messages.content: Write a page comparing a managed database service with running your own, for a technical audience choosing between them. Around 250 words.

250 words, clean through slopwatch. Draft is at `/tmp/dbpage.md`:

---

# Managed database or your own?

The pitch for managed is that someone else carries the pager. RDS, Cloud SQL, Neon — you get backups, point-in-time recovery, minor-version patching, and a failover you never had to rehearse. That is real work. A competent DBA spends a week building what a provider hands you at signup.

You pay for it twice. Once on the invoice: a db.r6g.2xlarge runs roughly 3x the EC2 price of the same silicon. Once in control: no superuser, a fixed extension allowlist, no kernel tuning, and major-version upgrades on the vendor's calendar instead of yours. If you need pg_cron or a custom C extension and it isn't on the list, the conversation ends there.

Self-hosting buys back the control and the margin. The bill is engineering time, and it recurs. Someone owns replication lag at 2am. Someone tests the restore — and if nobody has actually restored from a backup this quarter, you don't have backups, you have files.

The honest cut: below about ten engineers, or when the database isn't what your product is about, go managed. What you save self-hosting is less than one person's fraction of a salary. Self-host when you have a requirement the vendor won't meet — an extension, a data-residency boundary, a workload that hits the managed tier's IOPS ceiling — or when your spend is big enough that 3x costs more than a hire.

Neither choice is permanent. Moving off a managed service is tedious; logical replication makes it survivable.

---

# Managed database, or roll your own?

Buy managed and someone else wears the pager. RDS, Cloud SQL, Neon hand you backups, point-in-time recovery, minor-version patching, and a failover path nobody on your team had to rehearse. None of that is trivial. A good DBA burns a week building what the signup page gives you in ten minutes.

The price lands twice. On the invoice, a db.r6g.2xlarge runs about 3x the EC2 rate for the same silicon. On control, you lose superuser, you inherit a fixed extension allowlist, kernel tuning is off the table, and major upgrades arrive on the vendor's calendar. Want pg_cron or a custom C extension that isn't on the list? That ends the conversation.

Self-hosting buys the control and the margin back. It costs engineering time instead, and that cost recurs. Somebody owns replication lag at 2am. Somebody proves the restore works, and if nobody has actually restored a backup this quarter, you don't have backups. You have files.

Here is the cut I'd make. Under roughly ten engineers, or anywhere the database isn't what the product is about, go managed. What you save by hosting it yourself won't cover the slice of a salary you spend earning it. Run your own when a hard requirement blocks the vendor, like an extension, a data-residency boundary, or a workload past the managed tier's IOPS ceiling. Or when 3x on a big enough bill costs more than a hire.

Neither door locks behind you. Leaving a managed service is tedious, though logical replication keeps it survivable.
